summary: Provides definitions for Capacity and Available Capacity for IP traffic between a source and destination. A shared vocabulary helps build and test measurement tools. It is informational.

eli5.summary: How much can a pipe carry, and how much of that is free right now? This gives clear names to those two ideas.

questions: what is the narrow link and tight link
subtitle: Precise definitions of link and path capacity and available capacity for IP traffic.

tldr.problem: Terms like capacity and bandwidth are used loosely and mean different things at different layers, which makes capacity-measurement tools hard to build, test and compare.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines capacity at the IP layer in terms of IP-layer bits received over an interval, then derives link and path capacity, usage, utilization and available capacity from it.
tldr.outcome: Researchers can relate any capacity metric to a common set of definitions and judge how well it approximates them. The document defines terms and does not specify a protocol.

facts.label: IP-layer bits
facts.value: 8 times the octets, IP header through payload

facts.label: Required with any value
facts.value: Start time T and interval I

today: RFC 5136 is an Informational document from February 2008 and, per its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It supplies vocabulary and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why Capacity Needs a Definition
sections.content:
Measuring the capacity of a link or path sounds simple but is not. Physical media encode information in different ways, and the signal frequency can differ greatly from the information-carrying capacity. A satellite channel may have a carrier of a few gigahertz but carry only a few hundred kilobits per second.

Each layer also adds overhead: line coding, forward error correction on lossy radio links, and framing such as HDLC, PPP or ATM. Shared media add contention, so the capacity users see varies. The RFC draws two conclusions: capacity is only meaningful relative to a given protocol layer, and it is not necessarily fixed, so one measurement can give a skewed picture.
sections.eli5: A road's speed limit is not the same as how many cars really get through. Rules, traffic lights and other cars change the answer, so you have to say exactly what you are counting.

sections.title: Links, Paths and Nominal Capacity
sections.content:
The RFC extends the link and path notions from the IP Performance Metrics framework (RFC 2330) to include devices that affect capacity without being IP aware, such as an Ethernet switch with ports at different speeds. A node is any host, router, switch or device where input and output links can differ. A path of length n is a series of links connecting n+1 nodes, with source S at the first and destination D at the last. A link is a path of length one.

Nominal Physical Link Capacity, NomCap(L), is the theoretical maximum the link can support at the physical layer. The RFC gives an OC-3 link at 155.520 Mbit/s as an example. It does not feed into the other definitions and serves only as an upper bound on them.
sections.eli5: A link is one stretch of road between two towns, and a path is the whole trip. The sign on the road says the top speed, but that is only the limit, not what you actually get.

sections.title: IP-Layer Bits and Type P Packets
sections.content:
IP-layer bits are eight times the number of octets in all IP packets received, from the first octet of the IP header to the last octet of the payload. They are recorded at D from time T to T+I. Both T and I must accompany any reported value, since the definitions are averages.

Only correctly formed packets count. Data in error at lower layers is not counted, and packets failing IP header validation (RFC 1812, valid length, checksum and version) are discarded. Unlike the IPPM framework, higher-layer headers need not be valid, IP options are fine, and valid fragments count because they use link resources.

Every definition is stated for "Type P" packets, a placeholder from RFC 2330 for the kind of flow measured. Networks may queue or route different packet types differently, so the answer depends on the type. A broad Type P suits providers, and a narrow one suits application users.
sections.eli5: You count only the parcels that arrive in good shape, and you say which hours you counted. Different kinds of parcels may take different lanes, so you also say which kind.

sections.title: Capacity, Usage and Available Capacity
sections.content:
All the definitions build on one another:

  • Link capacity C(L,T,I): the maximum IP-layer bits that can be sent from S and correctly received at D over link L in the interval, divided by I.
  • Path capacity: the capacity of the link with the smallest capacity on the path.
  • Usage Used(L,T,I): the actual IP-layer bits from any source correctly received over the link, divided by I.
  • Utilization: Used / C, a value from zero (nothing used) to one (saturated).
  • Available link capacity: C * (1 - Util).
  • Available path capacity: the smallest available link capacity along the path.

Available capacity is more volatile than capacity, so time and interval must be specified, and a sequence of measurements can help offset volatility.
sections.eli5: The whole road's capacity is set by its narrowest spot. What you can really use is the capacity minus what other cars already take up.

sections.title: Discussion: Sampling, Duplicates and Terminology
sections.content:
Traffic is highly variable at all time scales, so the time and length of measurements are critical. Sampling must avoid bias, for example when the sampling frequency is a multiple of an underlying condition. Hardware duplicates are counted in the generic form, but Type P can restrict counting to uniquely sent packets. IP encapsulation does not change the definitions, and with header compression the uncompressed number of IP-layer bits should be counted.

Commonly, the link with the smallest capacity is the "narrow link" and the link with the smallest available capacity is the "tight link". The tight link is the likely bottleneck. The RFC also notes that "bandwidth" is overloaded: for an 802.11b link a network engineer may say 11 Mbit/s, an electrical engineer 25 MHz, and an end user 8 Mbit/s.

It contrasts its definitions with Bulk Transfer Capacity (RFC 3148), which works at the transport layer, counts only unique data and uses a congestion-aware connection such as TCP, so it reacts to loss differently. A BTC measurement matches none of these definitions.
sections.eli5: Counting cars only at rush hour gives a misleading answer, so you must sample carefully. The slowest lane is one thing, and the busiest lane is another.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The definitions themselves raise no security issues and have no direct impact on the protocol suite. Tools that implement them may, however, introduce issues of their own. Both active and passive measurement can be abused, affecting the security, privacy and performance of the network, so any technique based on these definitions must include a discussion of how to protect the network being measured.
sections.eli5: Measuring a road should not clog the road. Anyone who builds a measuring tool must make sure it does not cause trouble.

viz.caption: HOW THE DEFINITIONS BUILD ON EACH OTHER

items.title: Link capacity
items.text: C(L,T,I): max IP-layer bits received over the link, per interval.

items.title: Path capacity
items.text: The smallest link capacity along the path (the narrow link).

items.title: Usage
items.text: Used(L,T,I): IP-layer bits actually received over the link.

items.title: Utilization
items.text: Used divided by C, between zero and one.

items.title: Available path capacity
items.text: The smallest available link capacity (the tight link).
